title: POC scoping: cost modeling with Tesseract Labs
summary: Discovery / POC scoping focused on unit economics for a chat/assistant workload. Customer wants 95th %-ile latency under 300ms, < $0.0008 per token target for production, and a 6-week pilot with benchmarks comparing hosted vs dedicated. Action items include Redwood sending pricing and SOC2 + KMS docs, engineering schedule for benchmark windows, and defining success criteria and sample traffic shape.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-06 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes | Attendees: Maya, Liam (Redwood) — Priya, Daniel, Sara (Tesseract)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Liam our SE, we'll run through your POC scoping for cost modeling. Can you quickly re-introduce and confirm goals?
[00:12] Priya: Yeah hi, Priya Nair, Head of ML at Tesseract. Main goal is to understand per-token economics for our customer service assistant and figure out whether Redwood hosted or dedicated makes sense for us within our budget.
[00:25] Daniel: Daniel Kim, platform, I'll own infra for the pilot. We have strict residency and KMS requirements, and also want estimate on batching knobs and expected concurrency.
[00:35] Sara: Sara Lopez, CTO, quick note — timeline is tight, we want an internal demo and decision by mid January, ideally pilot start in late Jan.
[00:44] Liam: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: go over workload profile, define success criteria, run through benchmark plan and unit economics, then next steps.
[00:55] [00:55] Maya: Priya can you describe the workload shape? average request length, prompt vs generation tokens, percent of streaming responses?
[01:07] Priya: Sure, so it's customer support chat — avg prompt ~80 tokens, avg completion 120 tokens, about 30% of flows use tool-calling and structured output. Peak concurrency around 120 QPS internally but production target initially 40 QPS, bursty with diurnal spikes. 20% of requests are short FAQ-style under 50 tokens. We also care about 95th perc latency under 300 to 400 ms for web UX.
[01:40] Liam: Good detail. For cost modeling we look at tokens-in and tokens-out and also effective batching. If you can tolerate small extra latency we can batch to reduce per-token compute. Have you measured SLAs you need for cold vs warm cache?
[01:54] Priya: Warm latency we expect sub 200ms, but cold can be higher. The 95th percentile we mentioned earlier is the one we measure.
[02:05] [02:05] Maya: Ok on the economics side, we're going to estimate per-token cost under several profiles: hosted bursty, hosted with prefix/KV cache, and dedicated with quantized model. For a ballpark: on hosted with small efficient model we can hit around $0.0009 per generated token without aggressive batching; with batching and KV caching that dips to ~ $0.0005–$0.0006. On dedicated with int8 quantization you'd see lower unit costs but with committed monthly cost to amortize GPUs.
[02:44] Daniel: When you say KV caching are you caching the conversation prefix or the model weights? I want to be precise.
[02:50] Liam: Sorry, KV cache is the attention key/value cache — we mean prefix caching of repeated system prompts and conversation context so you don't re-run the full prompt, effectively reducing compute per-turn. Also we have prefix embeddings cache for reranking/embedding cases.
[03:06] Priya: And what's the tradeoff on memory footprint? Our instances are limited.
[03:11] Liam: Right, caching does increase memory, but for chat it usually pays off. For your avg 120 token responses, prefix cache can reduce compute by 35–50% on repeated flows. Memory footprint will depend on session count; we can scope that in the pilot.
[03:27] [03:27] Maya: On batching — for web UX 40 QPS you'd see room for batching within a 50–100ms micro-batch window if you can tolerate a 20–50ms added tail. For strict latency we keep batch sizes small and use continuous batching which trades off throughput. For cost modeling we show per-token cost at batch sizes 1, 4, 8.
[03:50] Daniel: Can you share example numbers for our profile?
[03:53] Liam: Quick example (rough):
- batch=1: $0.0012 / generated token
- batch=4: $0.00075 / generated token
- batch=8: $0.00055 / generated token
These are for hosted with a mid-sized open model; with KV cache you reduce the effective tokens processed and get to ~ $0.0004–$0.0006 at batch=8.
[04:20] Priya: That's helpful. Our cost target per token is around $0.0008 to start, because we need to stay under $X for unit economics. If hosted can't meet that we might look at dedicated.
[04:33] Maya: For dedicated, you need to include committed costs — e.g. a 4-GPU pool might be $Y/month plus orchestration. Effective per-token then depends on utilization. At 50% util you'd pay more per token than at 80–90% util. We'll produce a utilization vs unit-cost curve.
[04:52] [04:52] Sara: We have budget constraints — we can commit to a 6-week pilot with usage up to 10M tokens total, beyond that leadership wants clear ROI. So pilot should show path to $0.0006 or below per gen token.
[05:06] Liam: Ok, pilot scoping: we run two benchmark windows: hosted baseline with your sample traffic, and dedicated baseline if you want to spin one up. Benchmarks will measure latency p50/p95, cost per token assumptions, and regression tests against a set of eval prompts.
[05:22] Priya: For evaluation we have ~500 representative conversations and a stresstest set for concurrency. We'll share a sample dataset.
[05:30] Maya: Great. Technical questions — on compliance you mentioned KMS and residency?
[05:36] Daniel: Yes, keys must be within our cloud KMS (AWS KMS) and logs should be auditable. Also need SOC2 and data retention policies.
[05:45] Maya: We can support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated. For hosted we have an option for Bring-Your-Own-Key for certain enterprise plans; we'll include SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[05:57] [05:57] Priya: Any requirements for model quantization compatibility? We run some custom models and also open models from the catalog.
[06:05] Liam: Our runtime supports int8/4-bit quantization paths for many transformer weights. For custom models we do onboarding and we can test accuracy regressions. Quantization reduces GPU memory and often reduces cost 20–40% depending on model.
[06:19] Priya: We need to be careful about regen accuracy — we'll define thresholds in success criteria.
[06:24] Maya: Good point, success criteria should include both cost/latency SLOs and quality delta thresholds (e.g., <2% drop vs baseline on our eval set).
[06:34] [06:34] Liam: Proposed success criteria (tentative):
- p95 latency under 350ms for primary flows;
- per-generated-token cost <= $0.0008 on average across pilot;
- quality regression under 2% measured on your eval prompts;
- integration effort under 4 engineer-weeks to configure and run pilot.
[06:56] Priya: That aligns. Timeline?
[06:59] Maya: We can target benchmark run next week if you give sample traffic and a Slack channel for infra ops. Pilot launch (hosted) in 2 weeks, dedicated spin required 3–4 weeks including provisioning, so end-to-end decision by mid Jan fits.
[07:15] Daniel: We'll need a weekend window for high-concurrency test, and a runbook for fallbacks.
[07:21] Liam: We'll provide a benchmark runbook + test harness (scripted via k6 / locust / your choice) and a cost model spreadsheet where you can input concurrency, batch size, KV cache hit rate to compute per-token spend.
[07:35] [07:35] Priya: Could you share a sample cost calc?
[07:38] Maya: Yes I'll send an example spreadsheet and a couple of scenarios: hosted low-latency, hosted batched+cache, dedicated committed 4-GPU at 70% util. Also include sensitivity analysis for batch window +/-25ms, cache hit rate 0–60%.
[07:52] Daniel: On instrumentation, we need per-route token breakouts and trace ids to reconcile with billing.
[07:58] Liam: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and per-route dashboards; we'll enable a demo account so you can see that.
[08:07] [08:07] Sara: Any blockers for us to start? Tech debt or security approvals?
[08:11] Priya: We need SOC2 and KMS docs for procurement.
[08:15] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 and KMS integration docs. For pilot we'll sign an NDA and bring up a trial tenant.
[08:22] [08:22] Liam: Quick note — sometimes transcripts mislabel, so your engineering names may shift in the recording, but we'll supply clean artifact.
[08:30] Maya: Ok final recap and next steps in a minute.
[08:34] [08:34] Priya: Quick question about fallbacks — if dedicated pool saturates, can we overflow to hosted?
[08:40] Liam: Yes, smart routing supports fallback to hosted or smaller model variants; we'll include fallback policies in the pilot config. There's a small egress cost for cross-route.
[08:51] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pricing + SOC2 + KMS docs, benchmark harness, and cost model spreadsheet. Tesseract to share sample conv dataset (500 examples), stress test window preferences, and confirm pilot contact list. Schedule: benchmark next week, pilot start in 2 weeks, decision mid-Jan.
[09:15] Priya: Sounds good.
[09:18] Sara: We'll review and aim to send files tomorrow.
[09:21] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.
[09:25] [09:25] End of call.

Note: transcription contains typical ASR artifacts; speaker labels may be approximate. Some numeric placeholders (Y, X) used where exact pricing needs internal quote.
